articles.title: Haitian migrants changed this town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
articles.summary: The president thrust Springfield, Ohio, into the spotlight with a false pet-eating claim - years later, it remains at the heart of the immigration debate.
articles.body:
In this closely fought midterm election campaign, the small town of Springfield, Ohio, has become a symbol of modern America. But it is a symbol that changes dramatically depending on who is describing it.

To President Donald Trump, Springfield crystallises America's problems due to years of unchecked immigration. He once echoed a false claim that Haitian immigrants were eating pets here. Today, he says his mass deportation drive means its people are "getting their town back".

But to others, Springfield represents a well-known cycle in the story of modern America. The decline of traditional industry, followed by a spike in immigration fuelled by cheap housing and low-paid labour. It is a familiar tale across the country.

This story contains some distressing details

Pierre Damas Bel, 20, arrived in Springfield to join his father and stepmother in 2024.

He fled his native Haiti, which was gripped by political instability and gang warfare. He entered the US with the government's permission under a now-defunct Biden-era programme for migrants waiting in Mexico.

Bel, according to a family friend, then received a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS), which gives vetted individuals the right to live and work in the United States.

TPS usually lasts 18 months but is routinely rolled over, often for years, if the danger remains in the affected country.

Bel aspired to build a life in America, the friend said. He was an honours student, talented athlete and cadet in a high school programme training students to become officers in the US Armed Forces.

But in June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.

Bel was told to report to an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) field office where he was fitted with an ankle monitor which is used to track migrants facing deportation.

He wrote on Instagram that he felt "shame and humiliation" at having to wear the tag. And on 31 August, he parked his car on the side of a highway near Springfield, walked into oncoming traffic and was killed.

His family blamed his death on his feelings at having to wear the ankle monitor.

The Department for Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to questions from the BBC about Bel's case. ICE has previously rejected "any attempt to blame ICE for the death".

"Remaining in the country illegally, while fighting removal, is a choice. Leaving with a free flight home and $2,600 is also a choice," a spokesperson told US media earlier this year when asked about the case.

In the weeks before his death, Bel attended a Springfield support centre for Haitians facing deportation.

Its co-founder, Viles Dorsainvil, told the BBC that Bel had been in the process of filing a motion asking ICE to remove the tag.

"He went twice to the ICE facilities… begging them to remove the ankle monitor," he said. "He did everything right to be here until they put the tag on him."

In total, more than a million immigrants from 13 countries have had TPS terminated by the Trump administration. The changes meant many went from being legal to unauthorised migrants overnight.

In 2024, Trump made securing the border and the mass deportation of undocumented migrants core pledges in his election campaign. Polls suggest the border policy continues to have strong support among Republicans, but the nature of his immigration enforcement campaign has seen a drop in backing this year.

Ohio has become a swing state in the coming midterm Congressional elections, and one of two Republican-held Senate seats is up for grabs. Trump has visited the state twice already in an attempt to rally turnout and counter a slide in his approval ratings.

At a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, earlier this month, Trump returned to the topic of Springfield.

"You have a little town, beautiful little town in Ohio where they dropped about 35,000 Haitians. Well, they're being taken out and they're almost going to be gone and we're giving their town back," he said to cheers.

The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in its favour in the summer.

"The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty," James Percival, the general counsel for the Department of Homeland Security, said after the court's ruling. "This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."

In a social media post in August, the Department of Homeland Security posted a video of Haitians in chains wearing white uniforms being led onto a deportation flight. The video, accompanied by jaunty music, told Haitians whose TPS had expired to "LEAVE IMMEDIATELY".

The Trump administration has said it is conducting law enforcement operations in the town to keep Americans safe. It has also argued that Haiti is safe enough to return to.

The country is subject to the US State Department's highest Level 4 "Do Not Travel" danger warning.

The signs of decades of economic decline are still visible in Springfield, through shuttered factories and boarded up homes.

This part of the American Midwest was hit badly by last century's de-industrialisation, when those laid off from its once prolific factories sought work on the coasts or migrated to warmer, southern states.

Within the last five years, a Haitian population estimated to be around 20,000 strong arrived in the town. Many fled the devastating earthquake in 2010. Others left Haiti in 2021 during the violence and unrest that followed President Jovenel Moise's assassination.

It meant Springfield's population increased rapidly. With their legal status under TPS, many Haitians took on low-paid jobs in factories and distribution warehouses.

Rick Johnson, who served in the Marines, has a porch adorned with flags. The Stars and Stripes flutter close to a banner for the US Navy and another for the Marine Corps.

Johnson's wife served in the Navy while he was in the Marines at Camp Pendleton in California. Outside of his service, he has lived in Springfield his whole life. He made it clear he is a strong supporter of ICE's deportation drive.

"You get where we're coming from," he said. "We love America, we love Americans - any kind of Americans, but you kind of have to be American."

Johnson moved into this neighbourhood a decade ago, but he said the loss of industry has left much of it empty. "They've torn down every house around me, I don't really have any neighbours," he said. "The only neighbours I have are Haitians right here and they don't really bother me."

They moved in around four years ago, Johnson added, "but there's a lot of them". He referenced "the driving problems".

This is a view shared by other residents in Springfield - a perception that traffic accidents increased after the Haitian community arrived.

In 2023, an 11-year-old boy, Aiden Clark, was killed when his school bus overturned in a crash with a minivan. The van driver, Herman Joseph, originally from Haiti, did not have a valid US driver's licence and was jailed.

Aiden's father, Nathan Clark, later spoke at a Springfield City Commission meeting where he denounced politicians for using his son's death as a "political tool" to fuel anti-immigrant sentiment, saying his son was accidentally killed.

Johnson's concern is about the numbers and the speed of change. "Really it's the amount of them," he told the BBC. "If you come here you [should] come here legally. The Temporary Protected Status is done… it's time to go."

At a nearby grocery store run by Paschur Castelly, who left Haiti 20 years ago, most of the shelves are empty, except for those stocking religious candles and framed pictures of Catholic saints popular with this devout community.

"I can't purchase new merchandise because I don't have people coming in," he said.

"So, our communities, we have doctors, we have engineers… we came here to get a better life, to help our family in Haiti, you know? Our country doesn't offer us security."

After 20 minutes in the store, the first customer arrived. The man, who asked to remain anonymous, said he had been a warehouse worker for three years.

But like others who have lost TPS, it is likely to mean he has also lost the right to work.

As he chatted with Castelly, he pulled up his right trouser leg and revealed a large ankle monitor.

ICE has said these are part of its Alternatives to Detention programme. "I was given a choice, wear the ankle monitor and report in every two weeks, or sign my deportation order," he said.

As we left the store, Castelly closed the door which he now keeps locked. When a neighbour spotted us and feared an ICE raid, she shouted over to ask if Castelly was okay.

It was a sign of just how much this town remains a symbol - of two versions of America - years after Trump thrust it into the national spotlight, and weeks before voters head to the polls to shape the remainder of his presidency.

articles.title: Faecal waste pollutes drinking water in Mexico’s Yucatan, Greenpeace says
articles.summary: The report says nearby pig farms and municipal wastewater are the likely sources of contamination.
articles.body:
Faecal bacteria are contaminating water in wells and sinkholes in Mexico’s Yucatan state, which are a vital source of drinking water, according to a report by Greenpeace, a global environmental organisation.

The report, published on Tuesday, said nearby pig farms and municipal wastewater were likely sources of the pollution in the southeastern coastal state.

“A range of chemical and microbiological indicators reveal a complex mosaic of severe, localised organic pollution,” it said.

Greenpeace called for an immediate moratorium on new industrial livestock operations and farm expansions in the peninsular state, which was once home to the ancient Maya civilisation.

With no above-ground rivers, groundwater is the Yucatan’s only freshwater source, and the area’s porous limestone bedrock lets pollutants quickly seep into the aquifer.

The global environmental watchdog group commissioned an independent laboratory to test water at 17 sites near the state capital, Merida, in August.

The sites included household and farm wells, community water points and cenotes, the natural sinkholes that dot the Yucatan Peninsula, which is one of Mexico’s most popular tourist destinations.

According to the report, every sample showed some degree of contamination likely linked to faecal waste, and several sites appeared heavily polluted. Total coliform bacteria reached the test’s upper limit in 16 of 17 samples, and faecal coliforms did so in 13.

However, the tests cannot show whether the waste came from people or animals, and leaking septic tanks and municipal sewage may also contribute to contamination.

Greenpeace said, however, that separate testing using Pig2Bac, a pig-specific DNA marker method, detected pig faecal matter in samples analysed at laboratories at Johns Hopkins University in the US and Mexico’s National Autonomous University (UNAM).

Greenpeace said the results raise “critical accountability questions” about nearby pig farms.

Maya communities joined Greenpeace in demanding action from environmental authorities over the contamination.

A UN report published in July found that there are more than 500 industrial pig farms across Yucatan state with more than 50,000 animals, many located near the lands and territories of Indigenous Peoples.

Marcos Orellana, a former UN special rapporteur who authored the report, said waste and chemicals from industrial farms “find their way very quickly” into the water communities use for bathing, cooking and drinking. He said most farms lack required permits and that regional government initiatives “remain insufficient”.

“The contamination of the waters that have sustained Mayan culture for millennia is predominantly coming from the industrial operations of the growth of animals,” Orellana said.

But Antonio Zumarraga, vice president of the Yucatan Citizen Scientific Water Observatory, defended the local pork industry, saying the sector has invested in water treatment and supports conservation programmes. He blamed local authorities for their inaction.

“It’s an issue that, as long as it doesn’t carry political weight for the government, they won’t do anything about it,” Zumarraga said.

The Yucatan state government was not available for comment, while Mexico’s national water commission, CONAGUA, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Merida’s Association of Pig Farmers also did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has declined to endorse Vice President JD Vance as his successor in the 2028 presidential election, despite Vance saying he
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has declined to endorse Vice President JD Vance as his successor in the 2028 presidential election, despite Vance saying he expects to receive Trump's backing if he decides to run.Asked whether he viewed Vance as his successor and the Republican nominee for 2028, Trump replied, “No.” He then described Vance as “a very capable” person, adding that there were several capable people who could potentially succeed him.Trump's remarks came after Vance said he believed the president would endorse him if he entered the race, while also acknowledging that he had not discussed the possibility with Trump.What Trump said about VanceDuring the exchange, Trump was asked directly whether he saw Vance as his political successor and the Republican Party's nominee in 2028. His response was an unambiguous “No”, followed by a more favourable assessment of the vice president's abilities.“But he is a very capable, You know you have a lot of capable people,” Trump said.The remarks stop short of ruling out Vance as a potential successor, but Trump did not commit to backing him for the Republican nomination.Vance expects Trump's backing but leaves room for a contestVance, meanwhile, said he believed Trump would endorse him if he decided to contest the 2028 presidential election.“Look, I think if I run, the president will endorse me,” Vance said during an interview.Asked whether Trump would endorse him immediately after an announcement, Vance said he expected to receive the president's support but acknowledged that he had not discussed the matter with him.“I would think so, but I don't know, man. I haven't talked to him about it,” Vance said.He also suggested that Trump's endorsement would not necessarily need to determine the outcome of the Republican nomination contest.“I mean, again, I think I would get his endorsement. But I also think there's something to be said for people actually running their own race,” Vance said.He added that Trump's endorsement carried considerable weight and that the president could allow the nomination contest to unfold without backing a candidate at the outset.“Because the president's endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, you know what we need? Let this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.”The contrasting remarks leave Trump's position on the 2028 Republican race unclear. articles.title: Italy approves sweeping security measures in response to protests
articles.summary: Italy’s government approves sending 500 troops to Milan after clashes and protests.
articles.body:
Italy has approved the deployment of troops and tougher legal penalties in a bid to quell cost-of-living protests in the north of the country that occasionally turned violent over the weekend.

The Italian cabinet on Tuesday approved sending 500 troops to Milan, a new legal offence covering violent participation in a demonstration, tougher penalties for rioters and financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.

Italy’s Ministry of Defence said the military will help reinforce security at key sites, step up surveillance of sensitive locations and enhance monitoring.

Unrest swept northern Italian cities at the weekend, including the financial capital Milan, where groups of mainly young people looted shops, smashed windows and clashed with the police. The demonstrations were driven by anger over soaring fuel and energy prices, high rents, low wages and the state of public services.

As part of the new legal measures, which take effect immediately, anyone who takes part in a group of at least five people and endangers public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of €20,000 ($22,460).

Penalties increase if faces are concealed or people are injured.

Authorities can order prompt compensation for any damage inflicted and, in the case of minors, hold their parents liable.

Police will be allowed to detain youths aged between 14 and 17, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.

But the cabinet did not approve giving soldiers policing powers, as expected, after opposition from President Sergio Mattarella, Italian media reported.

“Destroying and stealing is not protest, it is crime, and the state’s response must be firm,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said in a social media post after the cabinet meeting.

The disturbances in northern Italy echoed riots in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent turmoil in years.

Meloni’s government is also facing mounting pressure from a separate wave of protests in southern Italy, where truck drivers angered by soaring diesel prices and the rising cost of living have staged roadblocks that are disrupting supply chains.

Protesters in both the north and the south say rising prices are pushing families into poverty, a concern for Meloni ahead of the 2027 national elections.

articles.title: 'Human rights shouldn't be used for political pressure': India amid UN criticism over handling of protests
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday asserted that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective targeting of countries,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday asserted that human rights should not be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective targeting of countries, opposing attempts to turn allegations and incomplete statistics into a “negative characterisation” of the world's largest democracy.While speaking at UNGA Third Committee, deputy secretary in the ministry of external affairs Barkha Tamrakar said, "Human rights not to be used as an instrument of political pressure or selective country targeting.""India engages with international human rights mechanisms, but such engagement must be based on dialogue, consultation, cooperation with non-selectivity and transparency as guiding principle," she added."We call on delegations to cite the report faithfully, not to inflate a humanitarian communication into a verdict."She also opposed any "attempt to convert unverified allegations, incomplete statistics or a report that contains no India country observation into a negative characterisation of the world's largest democracy".Remarks come amid UN experts’ concerns over protestsTamrakar's remarks came amid concerns raised by UN human rights experts over recent youth-led protests in New Delhi.On Tuesday, more than 20 UN human rights experts in Geneva expressed alarm over what they described as a “repeatedly heavy-handed police response” to peaceful youth-led demonstrations in the national capital.In a statement shared by UN special procedures, the experts alleged that law enforcement agencies had used force against unarmed students, detained protesters arbitrarily and imposed broad restrictions on public gatherings. They called on Indian authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly and ensure accountability for alleged abuses.“Despite the non-violent nature of the assemblies, law enforcement has deployed force against unarmed students,” the experts said.UN experts flag mass detentions, alleged ill-treatmentThe experts said hundreds of thousands of students and their supporters had gathered peacefully across the country to protest government decisions concerning the education system and, more recently, voter-roll deletions.They referred to reports that the deletions affected 130 million individuals, reportedly belonging to Muslim, Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities.According to the statement, more than 7,000 young people, journalists, human rights defenders, lawyers and political party members were recently detained in New Delhi and taken to detention centres farther away. Their phones were allegedly seized and protest-related material deleted. Most were released after 24 hours, including protest leaders, the experts said.The statement also cited reports of injuries and ill-treatment among protesters, expressing particular concern over allegations of sexual violence and other forms of gender-based abuse during demonstrations and related detentions.The experts also raised concerns over the reported use of Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) to impose broad restrictions on public gatherings, suspend public transportation and enforce internet shutdowns.They said restrictions on peaceful assembly must be lawful, pursue a legitimate objective and be necessary and proportionate.They urged Indian authorities to immediately stop the excessive use of force, lift blanket restrictions on assemblies and refrain from the misuse of digital surveillance, including biometric monitoring and internet disruptions.The UN experts called for an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the conduct of law enforcement personnel and affiliated forces, urging authorities to ensure accountability, justice and reparations for victims.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: More trouble for CJP leaders: Another FIR against Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka transferred to Crime Branch
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police has transferred a second FIR registered against Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to the Crime
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police has transferred a second FIR registered against Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to the Crime Branch, which will now investigate both cases linked to the activists' alleged entry into Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, sources said on Wednesday.Two cases were registered on October 13 following protests by CJP members at the two locations without approval, according to news agency ANI.The case related to Connaught Place was transferred to the Crime Branch on Tuesday, while the second case, concerning Jantar Mantar, has also now been handed over to the unit, sources said.According to news agency PTI, the police alleged that Das, Ranka, Ajinkya Shinde and 11 other CJP members entered the Jantar Mantar area on October 13 by trespassing through private premises. Jantar Mantar has been denotified as a designated protest site.Police personnel deployed at the spot intervened, and all 14 people were detained. Two FIRs were subsequently registered.CJP leaders move Delhi High Court against custody extensionMeanwhile, Das and Ranka have approached the Delhi High Court challenging an order extending their judicial custody, arguing that their continued detention despite furnishing sureties violates their fundamental right to personal liberty.Their legal team has challenged the October 19 order passed by a Special Executive Magistrate in New Delhi district under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).According to their lawyers, the magistrate rejected fresh sureties submitted by the two leaders on October 19 and directed them to explain why there should not be an apprehension of a breach of peace.The legal team contends that the continued detention is arbitrary and contrary to established legal principles. The leaders have sought the setting aside of the order, arguing that their detention infringes their constitutional right to personal liberty under Article 21.The matter is scheduled to be taken up by the High Court on Wednesday.The leaders sought an urgent hearing on Tuesday, including a night hearing, as the High Court remains closed for the Dussehra vacation.CJP legal affairs head Ratna Singh said in a post on X, "We have moved the Delhi high court and requested an urgent night hearing. Saurav and Ashutosh should not spend a single minute behind bars. Their liberty must not be curtailed because of political games. Justice must not wait."The party has alleged that bail proceedings have been deliberately delayed to prevent the release of its two co-convenors, the newspaper reported.Detentions began on October 10According to their legal team, Das and Ranka were first detained on October 10 after arriving at Terminal 3 of the Indira Gandhi International Airport. Preventive proceedings were initiated against them the following day, after which they were released on executing bonds of Rs 50,000 each.They were detained again on October 13 after going to Jantar Mantar carrying the national flag. They were subsequently shown as arrested under Sections 126 and 170 of the BNSS on October 14.A Special Executive Magistrate sent the two leaders to five-day judicial custody on October 14 for allegedly breaching peace bonds. articles.title: Brian Stack: Family of prison officer shot dead by IRA to get state apology
articles.summary: Brian Stack was crossing a street in Dublin in 1983 when he was shot in the back of the neck and died 18 months later.
articles.body:
The family of a senior Irish prison officer murdered by the IRA is to receive a state apology on Wednesday for failings in investigations into his killing.

Brian Stack, a father of three, was crossing a street in Dublin, after leaving a boxing match in 1983, when he was shot in the back of the neck.

Stack, who was the chief prison officer at the high-security Portlaoise Prison, was left paralysed and died 18 months later, aged 49.

There were three separate garda (Irish police) investigations into Stack's death, but no-one was brought to justice for his killing. On Wednesday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin will offer an apology on behalf of the state during a sitting of the Dáil (Irish parliament).

Apology will give 'great sense of comfort'

Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme Brian Stack's son, Austin Stack, said the apology "means an awful lot to us".

"It's a great sense of comfort, to particularly my mother and to myself and my two brothers, because the state is officially owning up to the errors and the missions that happened," he said.

He went on to say that the serious crime review team looked into the first investigation and "they found 194 errors and omissions".

"So I have, and my family have, met with several ministers for justice down through the years and we have a requested sight of that report.

"And every time we've requested it, we've been told that it's an internally valid document and that we cannot see it."

Austin Stack said that Wednesday would be a very emotional day for his family.

"My dad was doing a very difficult job at a very difficult time in our history," he said.

"He was awarded the Irish Prison Service's highest bravery award for that work that he was doing. And this is further vindication of him and his good name."

Prior to the Dáil proceedings, the Stack family will hold a private meeting at government buildings with the taoiseach and Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan.

The IRA admitted killing Stack in 2013 after his family mounted a long campaign to secure the admission, and met Sinn Fein's Gerry Adams and a former IRA commander.

Adams, at that time, expressed his "regret" to the Stack family over the killing.

In 2019, the family received an apology from then garda commissioner Drew Harris in relation to the handling of the investigation into the murder.

In 2023, gardaí told the family that the file on the case - which was with the DPP (Director of Public Prosecutions) - was being sent back to police for further investigation.

Stack was the only prisoner officer in the state killed by violence related to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Wimpole Estate records 'abundance' of wildlife despite drought
articles.summary: Wimpole's "long-term approach to nature recovery" has seen more than 5,000 species recorded.
articles.body:
A country house and farming estate in one of England's driest and most nature-depleted areas has an "abundance" of wildlife with more than 5,000 species recorded, the National Trust has said.

Rare species, including barbastelle bats, great crested newts and corn buntings, have been spotted at the Wimpole Estate in Cambridgeshire in the last six years.

General manager David Hassall said the number was "remarkable in any landscape, but particularly here in Cambridgeshire, where wildlife is facing the combined pressures of habitat loss and increasingly hot, dry conditions".

The government said the East was one of seven UK areas in drought , with hosepipe bans in force across parts of the region.

The charity said 5,242 species were recorded across the estate's parkland, farmland, woodland and wetlands.

Hassall said the number "reflects five decades of careful stewardship and shows that nature can flourish alongside farming, public access and heritage conservation".

Since 2021, the National Trust said it had planted 125,000 trees and created 35 hectares of woodland and 52 hectares of wood pasture, with another 77 hectares of tree planting currently being designed.

Species recorded also included a tiny pygmy ant, which the charity said was recorded at only one other UK site.

Ben McCarthy, head of nature conservation at the National Trust, said: "Across the UK, wildlife is under immense pressure from habitat loss and fragmentation as well as climate change, making the need to restore nature more urgent than ever.

"Places like Wimpole demonstrate the value of taking a long-term approach to nature recovery.

"By creating and restoring habitats across whole landscapes, we can provide more space for wildlife and help reverse decades of decline."

articles.title: The Weather Catcher:  Children use drawings to explore mental health for Book Week NI
articles.summary: A group of primary school pupils have turned their ideas about feelings and emotions into a book.
articles.body:
A group of primary school pupils have come together to turn their ideas about feelings and emotions into a book designed to help young people understand their mental health.

The Weather Catcher was co-created by Year Six pupils from Glencraig Integrated Primary School and Holywood Primary school, using weather to help children understand that feelings can change from day to day.

Through a series of workshops organised by Action Mental Health, Illustrator Ellan Rankin guided the children to use colours, shapes and textures to represent their emotions.

The book is being launched on Love Your Library Day which coincides with Book Week NI.

Eleven-year-old Rafferty said he drew inspiration from colours and elements of nature to convey different feelings.

"I thought of things like the sea, rain and blue objects, because sometimes sadness can be associated with blue and rain."

A keen reader, Rafferty enjoys novels and said taking part in the project had given him an opportunity to explore his interest in storytelling.

"I've always wanted to be an author, but I didn't think I would start this young," he said.

Edith, 10, helped develop the book's message about happiness, and how good weather can influence people's feelings.

"When the weather was really nice and it was sunny, the characters felt really happy," she said.

"It kind of feels a little strange, to be honest, because you would never expect a ten-year-old to draw and find the drawing in a book," she added.

Edith hopes to see the finished drawings and some of her favourite characters, including a storm cloud designed by one of her friends.

Ten-year-old Merryn said reading was both enjoyable and calming and helped her develop her vocabulary.

"Sometimes I walk to the library after school and sometimes, I'll just read books at home," she said.

As part of the project, Merryn used shapes to represent different emotions.

"For anger, I think of squares and then happiness, probably triangles or just shapes, simple shapes like that," she said.

Merryn also contributed a cloud to the book, using it to represent anger and grumpiness. She said she was pleased to see her drawing included in the finished project.

Eleven-year-old Lizzie said she hoped the book would help young people recognise their own experiences and emotions in its characters.

"It's not every day you see a book written by people your age, with topics that you might feel are similar to your life," she said.

Lizzie described seeing the project come together as surreal.

"It's so weird to be saying: 'I did this'", she said.

She added that reading was important for young people, both in everyday life and as a way of developing their English skills.

Eleven-year-old Toby hopes the book will help other young people feel able to express their emotions.

"I think it's a really good book and it's really going to help people," he said.

Toby said expressing emotions was important, even when it might feel difficult.

"They can be quite useful and you should express them, even if you don't think you should," he said.

Illustrator Ellan Rankin said that she worked with the children over two days by connecting colour and shapes with a range of different emotions.

"They probably just thought these are just scribbles, but now hopefully that they see it in action, they'll understand what it was that they were doing."

Ellan, taking inspiration from the student's drawings, used photoshop to make a digital collage, bringing everything together and said how important it is for the young people to be involved in the project.

"I think talking about it from a really young age is very important to have it be socially acceptable"

David Babington from Action Mental Health described the project as wonderful.

Speaking about how reading habits have changed, he said he hopes the book will inspire younger readers to move from screens to pages.

"I hope that these children with this book will start to have that habit and start to think about reading more widely, not looking at screens all the time, but sitting down and looking at all the subjects that matter through a book."

articles.title: Massive wasps' nest in nature reserve office dismantled
articles.summary: The insects lived in a nature reserve office for four months.
articles.body:
A nature reserve manager has finally dismantled a large wasps' nest in her office after the insects made it their home for four months.

Eilish Rothney, a nature reserve manager for the Trinity Broads at the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, found wasps buzzing around the room in June, when she returned from conducting surveys.

The wasps had made their home on the shelves of the Ormesby St Michael office, wrapping around binders and other items. They left the nest a few weeks ago.

Rothney said: "It's kind of a fitting tribute that we've welcomed what many, many people see as a pest...and we've helped them survive, which will help this whole ecosystem that we rely on."

Rothney said that when she first saw the size of the nest in June it was about the size of a paperback book.

She added: "There was just like constant [wasps] coming and going, probably 10s, 20s in and out all the time."

Rothney started dismantling the nest on Tuesday and said that she knew in the autumn, it would be time for them to leave.

When she hadn't seen any wasps for a number of weeks she decided to explore by cutting away at the nest.

She said that she was "amazed" to peel back a number of layers before reaching the shelves. She added that it was not until she got closer to the ring binders that she could see "hexagonal cells where the larvae would have been".

Rothney said she'll miss her office colleagues, but she knows they'll be back and added: "I think if they do come back in here next summer they will be welcome".

Rothney said it was important that we make space for nature. She added: "Although people don't like them [wasps] are part of nature.

"They have a really, really important role to play, as do all the insects, even mosquitoes, which are not my favourite."

She said she thought the wasps struggled because of the warm summer. Due to her office being near a pond and a meadow, the wasps were able to get food and water.

articles.title: In 2017, Kaley Cuoco bought a 40-acre California ranch for $4.99 million; nine years later, the Big Bang Theory star's property has become a refuge for rescued horses, cows, goats, pigs and other animals
articles.summary: When Kaley Cuoco purchased a 40-acre property in California for $4.99 million in 2017, it already had facilities for keeping horses.
articles.body: When Kaley Cuoco purchased a 40-acre property in California for $4.99 million in 2017, it already had facilities for keeping horses. Nine years later, the ranch has become a refuge for rescued animals, including horses, cows, goats, pigs, donkeys and birds. The actress, who became widely known for playing Penny in The Big Bang Theory, has spent years developing the property to accommodate animals that need a home.Located in Thousand Oaks, northwest of Los Angeles, the ranch was originally designed for people interested in horse riding and keeping horses. According to Realtor.com, the property lies in the foothills of the Santa Monica Mountains and includes a three-bedroom, 2,720-square-foot house. It was advertised as an equestrian estate when Cuoco bought it, with a barn and arenas already available.But Cuoco had plans that went beyond keeping horses. Having grown up around them, she was familiar with caring for animals. As the years passed, she began taking in different species, including animals that had been rescued from poor living conditions and horses that had retired from racing.By 2024, the property had become an important part of both her animal rescue work and her family life. In interviews with People magazine that year, Cuoco spoke about the animals living there, the changes she had made to the ranch and why providing older animals with a safe home meant so much to her.Horse ranch becomes home for different animalsOne of the unusual features of Cuoco's property is that several different species share the same living areas. Rather than keeping every type of animal completely separate, she has created spaces where smaller farm animals can live together.These include goats, pigs, chickens, ducks, miniature horses and dwarf ponies. Cuoco said the animals gradually establish their own relationships and become comfortable sharing the space."We have a big area where most of the little animals go, the goats, pigs, chickens and mini horses, and they all live together," she said.In the same interview, she revealed that two turkeys had recently joined the ranch. She had wanted to rescue turkeys for some time and was delighted by how friendly the birds were.The property also houses cows, including two named Connie and Ronnie, as well as donkeys and larger horses. Some of the horses are Thoroughbreds that have finished their racing careers.Cuoco has made changes to the property to accommodate its growing animal population. These include building a petting zoo and developing the barn, where she has also installed contemporary chandeliers.Why older rescued animals are especially important to herNot every animal arriving at Cuoco's ranch is young or healthy. Some have experienced difficult circumstances before being rescued, while others are already in the later stages of their lives.Cuoco has said that watching these animals settle into their new surroundings is one of the most rewarding parts of running the ranch. She particularly values being able to care for older animals that may have fewer years left to live."We have taken animals out of terrible situations, and to see the growth in how they thrive here, they’re all so happy," she said.Her interest in animal rescue is also connected to her experience with dogs. Cuoco previously had a rescued pit bull mix named Norman, who died in 2021.She has named both her production company and her pet-care brand after him. The brand, Oh Norman!, sells products including dog bowls, treats, toys and clothing. Cuoco has said she wanted a portion of purchases to support animal rescue organisations.Ranch became part of her daughter's childhoodWhile Cuoco initially developed the ranch around her interest in animals, it has also become a place where she wants her daughter, Matilda, to grow up learning about them. She said she introduced her daughter to the horses when she was very young and had even kept a pony for her to ride when she became old enough.However, Cuoco does not consider riding essential. She believes that simply spending time around animals, helping care for them, and understanding their routines can be valuable experiences for a child.Cuoco shares Matilda with actor Tom Pelphrey, whom she began dating in 2022. Pelphrey also shares her interest in animals. Cuoco recalled that his photographs with a German shepherd had caught her attention before their relationship began. When he first visited the ranch, he was surprised by what she had created there.The property has since become a place where the couple and their daughter spend time together, away from Cuoco's work in the entertainment industry.Animal Cuoco still hopes to rescueDespite having a large collection of rescued animals, Cuoco has spoken about one species she would particularly like to add to the ranch. In the 2024 interview, she also said that rescuing a giraffe remained an ambition she had not yet fulfilled. "I am still dying to rescue a giraffe. We have not done that yet," she said.Cuoco has owned several California properties during her acting career, including homes in Sherman Oaks, Tarzana, Hidden Hills and Agoura Hills.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why did Sharmila Tagore insist on surgery for stage zero lung cancer, reveals Soha Ali Khan
articles.summary: Going for surgery is never an easy decision, especially for someone at the age of 81.
articles.body: Going for surgery is never an easy decision, especially for someone at the age of 81. Yet veteran actress Sharmila Tagore insisted on going for surgery after being diagnosed with lung cancer, even though many people felt that it was unnecessary. Sharmila Tagore had opened up about the incident in 2023 on Koffee with Karan, explaining why she couldn't be a part of his movie Rocky Aur Rani Kii Prem Kahaani.Recently, Soha Ali Khan, on her podcast All About Her, talked again about her mother's surgery. She mentioned that the veteran actor was diagnosed at stage zero, yet insisted on undergoing surgery.“It is very hard to diagnose early, and in her case, it was stage zero, and because she insisted on being cut open, a lot of people said it was unnecessary. She insisted, and it was only at that stage on the table that they said it was malignant and managed to cut it all out, which was one of the best-case scenarios for somebody with lung cancer,” Soha revealed on the podcast.What is stage zero lung cancer?According to the National Cancer Institute, USA, stage zero is when abnormal cells are found in the airways of the lungs and have not spread to the deeper lung tissues. If not identified, they may turn cancerous over time.In the case of Sharmila Tagore, her daughter explained how her decision to undergo the procedure proved significant. It was only on the operating table that doctors found the tissue to be malignant, and it was removed in time. This raises a serious concern about the diagnosis of cancer cells and why doctors may recommend surgery at a very early stage.Why is stage zero cancer difficult to detect?At stage zero, the tissue may not be cancerous, but the risk can be significant because doctors may not always know which lesions are likely to grow or spread and which could simply be monitored. This is relevant to the case of Sharmila Tagore.The more shocking part is that many early-stage lung lesions are asymptomatic, i.e., they do not cause any symptoms or warning signs. So, you can't rely on your body to tell you that the tissue is turning cancerous.This is why routine health screenings are important. Some early detections happen during routine checkups at the doctor's office.What happens if doctors detect a lump?If doctors find any suspicious lump in the body during a checkup, the next step is to investigate further. Depending on the type of cells and the growth, the next step is determined. This may require imaging tests such as CT scans or even a biopsy, in which a small part of the tissue is taken to a lab for examination under a microscope.The biopsy may reveal the type of tumour and whether it is malignant or abnormal, depending on which doctors can suggest surgery.This was previously the reason why many people felt that surgery was not required for the veteran actor, as the malignancy was not determined until she was in the operating room.Did Sharmila Tagore need chemotherapy after surgery?One of the encouraging aspects of Sharmila Tagore's recovery was that she did not require chemotherapy after the affected tissue was removed. Many people dread chemo, sometimes even before the treatment itself begins.As per CION Cancer Clinics, many patients find that their anticipation of chemotherapy worsens as the course progresses, even when the cycles themselves stay the same. Some may feel sick or anxious the moment they smell the treatment unit or even see the building.Repeated hospital visits, the fear of side effects and the disruption of everyday routines can make someone emotionally exhausted, to the point where a life-saving treatment journey becomes more difficult than the disease itself. This is why emotional support and medical guidance remain important throughout the process.Nevertheless, chemo remains an important and potentially life-saving treatment. Whether a patient needs it depends on the type of cancer, its stage and the findings from the examination of the removed tissue.Sharmila Tagore's experience shows how her decision to undergo surgery helped save her life. Not only this, but her case also serves as a reminder that every diagnosis is different. Understanding the condition, discussing treatment options with doctors and making informed decisions can help patients navigate a very difficult and exhausting journey. What the patient needs most is constant support from her loved ones.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Jackdaw approved but tricky energy trade-offs remain
articles.summary: Jackdaw and Rosebank are case studies in the slow motion awkwardness the UK has over energy.
articles.body:
The decision to grant approval for drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea and the further delay in a decision about the Rosebank oil field, also in the North Sea, are case studies in the slow-motion awkwardness the UK has collectively had, over years, about energy.

At the heart of that awkwardness, these questions: where should our energy come from, and with what costs and consequences, for the customer and for the environment?

Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has talked about a desire to be "pragmatic" about the North Sea as he puts it, which is why this decision about Jackdaw isn't a surprise.

In fact it felt near inevitable after President Trump blurted out – after his first phone call with Burnham in the summer – that the prime minister had told him he would "open up the North Sea".

Burnham acknowledged the two leaders had discussed the issue, arguing: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that."

What we now know is the government is approving drilling of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

A decision on Rosebank, an oil field about 80 miles north east of Shetland, is expected to take a bit longer.

UK government approves Jackdaw gas field and says production will start this month

The city caught in the middle of the big energy shift debate

The timeline of back and forth about both projects is worth revisiting. Jackdaw was first approved four years ago, Rosebank three years ago.

But after a legal challenge by environmental campaigners, it was ruled that consent had been granted unlawfully and there needed to be a more detailed assessment of the environmental impact.

And then, of course – there is politics, international and domestic, between parties and within parties.

Debate about energy security and spiralling prices, given the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the environmental impact, carbon emissions and the message new drilling sends to the wider world.

But others point to the extra carbon emissions when energy is imported, the tax revenues generated from domestic energy and the social and economic consequences of the British oil and gas sector deindustrialising too quickly and, in particular, the impact on cities such as Aberdeen.

Then, for the government, there are the promises the Labour Party made when it was seeking your support at the general election in 2024.

Page 52 of Labour's manifesto reads like a rhetorical twister – a paragraph of promises seeking to stretch in multiple directions at the same time, trying to keep a breadth of people happy simultaneously, or perhaps not annoy too many people too much.

"Labour will not revoke existing licences and we will partner with business and workers to manage our existing fields for the entirety of their lifespan. Crucially, oil and gas production in the North Sea will be with us for decades to come, and the North Sea will be managed in a way that does not jeopardise jobs," it reads.

"And our offshore workers will lead the world in the industries of the future. We will not issue new licences to explore new fields because they will not take a penny off bills, cannot make us energy secure, and will only accelerate the worsening climate crisis," it adds.

Crucially, the Jackdaw and Rosebank licences had already been issued, leaving political wriggle room on these two outstanding and high profile decisions the Labour government inherited on taking office.

But the multiple trade-offs, of course, remain very real, including for some of the key individuals involved.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who used to be the energy secretary, has long been vocal about what he sees as the need to move away from fossil fuels.

His successor, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who has announced this decision, previously wrote that "to have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can't have any new oil or gas fields," adding "it's irresponsible and short sighted to be funding new fossil fuels when we need to get to Net Zero fast."

Fahnbulleh has today told BBC Radio Scotland gas from Jackdaw will be "in our homes and businesses this month" but acknowledged that it "won't lower our energy bills this winter".

Instead, she is grounding her argument for approving this in energy security and saying the tax revenue generated will go into an "Energy Wealth Fund" to pay for "low carbon and renewable projects".

Rosebank, she added, was a "different proposition" as its oil would be exported, but she will "look at it".

What we can expect in the coming hours and days - as it has started already - is a resumption of all the arguments these projects have already provoked, with some saying approval should have happened ages ago, alongside plenty more.

And others arguing the announcement is utterly irresponsible.

articles.title: An Australian designer develops hempcrete tiles to recreate tree hollows and rocky crevices; shelters aim to help threatened wildlife, including eastern quolls and ringtail possums
articles.summary: Australian designer Xavier Earls has developed Bush Cradle, a modular wildlife habitat system made from hempcrete tiles that mimic natural shelters such
articles.body: Australian designer Xavier Earls has developed Bush Cradle, a modular wildlife habitat system made from hempcrete tiles that mimic natural shelters such as tree hollows, fallen logs and rocky crevices. The system is designed to help conservationists create customised refuges for native animals facing habitat loss. Its four interlocking tile designs can be assembled into different configurations, including tree hollows and ground dens, with entrances tailored to individual species. The project aims to address the shortage of natural shelter for wildlife, including eastern quolls and ringtail possums. In an encouraging early observation, ringtail possums reportedly used a prototype overnight, offering an initial indication of the design's potential.How hempcrete tiles recreate tree hollows and rocky crevicesBush Cradle uses four tile shapes connected through a slot-and-pin mechanism, allowing shelters to be assembled, dismantled and rearranged by hand without conventional tools. This makes it possible to adapt their configurations to different species and environments.The tiles are made from fibrous hempcrete, chosen for its insulating properties. Their manufacture combines 3D printing and casting, with lightweight printed frames placed inside moulds before hempcrete is poured in and left to cure. Laser-cut wooden entrance pieces allow openings to be customised for different animals.According to Earls' project description, the developed tiles weigh approximately 200 grams each, compared with early prototypes that weighed more than one kilogram. The modular design also allows individual components to be repaired or replaced without discarding an entire shelter.Why Australia's wildlife needs alternative sheltersNatural features such as tree hollows, fallen logs and rocky crevices provide essential places for animals to rest, nest, hide from predators and raise their young. However, land clearing, development and habitat degradation are reducing the availability of these refuges.Tree hollows are particularly important for many native species, but they can take hundreds of years to form naturally. When mature trees disappear, the animals that depend on their hollows can lose essential shelter long before replacement habitats develop.Bush Cradle offers a potential way to bridge this gap by allowing conservationists to construct artificial refuges suited to particular species and landscapes. Its adaptable components provide an alternative to conventional nest boxes, which are often designed for a specific purpose.Which animals could benefit from Bush Cradle?The system is intended to accommodate different native Australian animals by allowing shelters to be tailored to their habitat requirements.Eastern quolls: These spotted, nocturnal marsupials use dens and other sheltered spaces. Bush Cradle can be configured to mimic hollow logs and ground refuges, with entrances and chambers adapted to their needs.Ringtail possums: These tree-dwelling marsupials need protected places to rest. A Bush Cradle prototype installed in a tree was reportedly occupied by wild ringtail possums overnight.Other native wildlife: Earls has identified potential applications for pygmy possums, reptiles, endangered skinks and microbats. Different configurations could accommodate their varying entrance sizes and shelter requirements.Early field observations offer an encouraging signTrail-camera footage reportedly recorded ringtail possums using a Bush Cradle prototype installed in a tree overnight. The observation provided an early indication that the structure could serve as a usable refuge beyond the design studio.However, a single observation cannot establish whether the shelters improve long-term survival, breeding success or population recovery. Further monitoring would be needed to determine how consistently different species use the structures and how well they perform under varying weather conditions.Who developed Bush Cradle?Earls created Bush Cradle as his final-year industrial design project at Monash University in Australia. His work combines ecological research, digital modelling, 3D printing and material experimentation to explore how design could help address habitat loss.An internship at Reef Design Lab helped him explore how digital fabrication and casting could be combined to produce habitat structures. Earls now works full-time at the organisation, continuing to investigate how design can support ecosystems.Bush Cradle received a Best in Class Award in the Next Gen category at the 2026 Australian Good Design Awards, according to Monash University. The recognition highlighted the project's approach to combining industrial design with wildlife conservation.What comes next for the project?Earls aims to establish a network of conservationists who can use Bush Cradle to create customised wildlife refuges in Australia and potentially elsewhere. The project has also attracted interest for possible use in restoring habitat for endangered skinks and microbats in mining-affected areas of northern Queensland.The long-term ambition is to make artificial habitat creation more accessible, allowing conservationists to respond to the requirements of different species rather than relying on a single shelter design.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Get your facts straight’: BJP accuses Rahul Gandhi of hypocrisy over RSS remarks on women’s rights
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Wednesday hit back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks accusing the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Wednesday hit back at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks accusing the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) of gender inequality, with party leaders alleging hypocrisy and questioning his understanding of the organisation.BJP national spokesperson CR Kesavan accused the Raebareli MP of hypocrisy over his comments on respecting women, while party MLA Ram Kadam said the Congress leader should study the RSS before making allegations against it.Kesavan alleged that the Congress leader's remarks about treating women with respect were contradicted by his conduct towards a woman police personnel and a woman journalist."Rahul Gandhi sermonising about treating women with respect is indeed most sadistic and cruel given how Rahul Gandhi in the recent past has misbehaved improperly and inappropriately with both a female police personnel and a woman journalist," Kesavan said.He also questioned Rahul’s response to allegations against a Congress MP facing multiple charges of sexually harassing students."Rahul Gandhi's farcical remarks are highly hypocritical because if Rahul Gandhi truly even had an iota of respect for our women's power, Rahul Gandhi would have squarely condemned and taken action against the Congress MP who is now facing multiple charges of sexually harassing students," Kesavan said.The BJP spokesperson further accused the Congress of failing to advance women's empowerment during its years in power, claiming that the party had not passed the women's reservation Bill despite governing the country for more than 55 years at the Centre."Right from Nehru's Congress to Rahul Gandhi's Congress, the Congress party has always been against women empowerment which is why despite being in power for more than 55 years at the Centre, the Congress party never bothered to pass the women's reservation bill," he said.BJP questions Rahul Gandhi's understanding of RSSBJP MLA Ram Kadam also criticised Rahul's remarks, arguing that the Congress leader should verify his claims before making public statements about the RSS."Rahul Gandhi frequently makes remarks about the RSS. While he certainly has the right to engage in political accusations, counter-accusations, and sharp criticism, he should do so only after proper study," Kadam said.Questioning the former Congress president's claim about the organisation's treatment of women, Kadam said the RSS had a women's wing that operated across the country."Is he unaware that the RSS also has a wing for women? It operates across the entire country, and women work within it with the same level of prominence as men," he said.Kadam also questioned whether Rahul was making statements on social media without sufficient information."Are you going to tweet from your X handle based on incomplete information just to grab headlines? At the very least, get your facts straight. Tweeting with such a childish, immature mindset does not befit a leader of the opposition," he said.Telangana BJP chief targets Congress over women's reservationTelangana BJP state president N Ramchander Rao also accused Rahul of overlooking what he described as the male-dominated nature of the Congress. He challenged the party to explain its record on women's representation and support for the 33 per cent women's reservation proposal."Rahul Gandhi seems to be forgetting how male-dominated his party is. Wherever they are ruling, let him answer how many women chief ministers there are. This BJP has got a woman chief minister in the capital," Rao said.Questioning the Congress's position on women's reservation, he said, "If you are not anti-woman, then why don't you support 33% women reservation with delimitation? Your party failed to pass that legislation in the Parliament several times."Rao also challenged Rahul's claim that women supported his political fight against the RSS, arguing that the Congress's actions did not match its stated position on women's empowerment."Rahul Gandhi has claimed that women are with him, and 'smash patriarchy' is only a slogan for him. But in practice, Congress is against women," he said.Rao also raised the issue of a Congress MP who, he alleged, had been suspended and removed from service at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) over a sexual harassment case."What action have you taken against your own MP who has been suspended and removed from service in JNU over a sexual harassment case?... This is a hypocritical stance of the Congress party," he said.What Rahul Gandhi said about RSSThe BJP leaders were responding to a Rahul's post on X on Tuesday, in which the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha described the RSS as an "all-male, anti-constitutional cult" and alleged that it believed women were the property of men."The RSS is an all-male, anti-constitutional cult that believes women are the property of men. I believe in Shiva-Shakti. That's why it gives me such joy to fight them. What's beautiful is that many of their 'own' women are on my side," Rahul wrote.His remarks were the latest in a series of attacks on the RSS. articles.title: Witkoff in Russia for Putin meeting after ‘positive’ talks with Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio described Witkoff’s talks with Zelenskyy as ‘positive’, as efforts to end war intensify.
articles.body:
United States Special Envoy Steve Witkoff has arrived in St Petersburg for talks with Russian leaders on the Ukraine war following “positive” talks with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway.

Witkoff is due to meet President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday in the city in northwestern Russia, as the US pushes for an end to the war that began more than four and a half years ago with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump has expressed increasing frustration with Zelenskyy in recent weeks and has suggested that someone else should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf. The remarks signalled a new low in their relationship, while Zelenskyy has accused the US of suspending crucial intelligence sharing.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the talks between Witkoff and Zelenskyy as “positive”, adding that the US envoy would share the results with Putin. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner also attended the talks with Zelenskyy, but did so virtually because of illness. Kushner is also expected to attend the meeting with Putin remotely.

“He’ll now, armed with those ideas, be able to go to St Petersburg and share them with the Russian side – and let’s see if we can make some progress,” Rubio said.

The prime ministers of Norway and Finland also attended the talks in Oslo. Representatives from the European Union and NATO were present. Following Tuesday’s talks, Zelenskyy said “very, very important” intelligence from the US had been restored.

Zelenskyy has also accused Washington of slowing down the internet service, Starshield, which is crucial for Ukraine’s battlefield operations. Starshield is the military-grade equivalent of Starlink and is also developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Rubio dismissed Zelenskyy’s accusations, saying Trump had “nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield”. Musk disputes this and says such decisions can only be made by the US military and president.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown of the service, citing US officials and people familiar ⁠with the matter.

As diplomatic efforts intensify, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade long-range attacks.

At least one person was killed and two were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s western Bryansk ⁠region on Wednesday, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Telegram.

The Ukrainian Emergency Service said two people were killed in a Russian attack on a high-rise building in the Sviatoshinsky district of the capital, Kyiv.
